transcript.text: Hi, I'm Sensei. Put your page under the camera and start solving. I'm watching.
You found the friction force correctly. Can you explain why the normal force is equal to mg on an incline?
Um, because normal force is always the weight? I don't really know why.
Okay, let me think.

The normal force isn't always equal to the weight. On an incline, it's the part of the weight that pushes straight into the surface. Try a 10 kg block on a 30-degree slope: what part of its weight pushes straight down into the ramp?
I don't get it. Isn't all of the weight pushing down? How is only part of it?
Good question. One moment.
The weight pulls straight down, but only the part perpendicular to the slope pushes into the surface. Try a 10 kg block on a 30-degree slope: what part of its weight pushes straight into the ramp?
I don't know how to find that part. Like what do I multiply by?
Let me see.
The normal force is the part of the weight that pushes straight into the surface. On a 30-degree slope, you multiply the weight by the cosine of the angle. What is the cosine of 30 degrees?
Cos 30 is about 0.87. So N is 49 times 0.87, like 42.4? Then friction is 0.2 times that, 8.5 newtons?
Got it. Give me a second.

You're right that cos 30 is about 0.87, so the normal force is about 42.4 newtons. But you used the full weight, 49 N, instead of the part pushing straight into the ramp. Try again with the correct normal force.
I did use 42.4 though. 0.2 times 42.4 is 8.5 newtons. Is that right?
Okay, let me think.
The friction force is the coefficient times the normal force. You already found the normal force as the part of the weight pushing straight into the ramp. Try calculating friction using that number.
That's what I did. Friction is 8.5 newtons. I'm writing that down, thanks.
Good question. One moment.
You wrote N = mg, but on an incline, the normal force is less than the weight. Try again with the correct normal force.
